items.stem: An Olympic track cyclist of mass 160 kg rounds a Siberian-pine velodrome banking of horizontal radius 32 m banked at 14 ° to the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². At what design speed is zero lateral friction required along the slope?
items.workedSolution: With zero slope friction, N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = m v² / r. Dividing gives tan θ = v² / (g r), so v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.8 × 32 × tan 14°) = 8.84 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v = √(g r tan 14°) to obtain 8.84 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Assisted by lateral grip of static coefficient 0.35 on a banked oval speedway turn banked at 16 ° with radius 145 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻²), a 640 kg endurance prototype sports car moves at 25.9 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum safe cornering speed.
items.workedSolution: At maximum speed, limiting friction μ_s N acts down the slope: N(cos θ − μ_s sin θ) = mg and N(sin θ + μ_s cos θ) = m v_max² / r. Dividing yields v_max = √[g r (sin 16° + 0.35 cos 16°) / (cos 16° − 0.35 sin 16°)] = 31.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves N and down-slope μ_s N horizontally and vertically to obtain v_max = 31.7 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Sensors on an iced banked chute corner (radius 215 m, banking 25 °) measure the perpendicular load of a 880 kg bobsleigh cruising with zero side-friction. Using g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the normal reaction.
items.workedSolution: Because the circular path lies in a horizontal plane, vertical acceleration is zero: N cos θ = mg, so N = (880 × 9.81) / cos 25° = 9.53 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 25° = mg to obtain N = 9.53 × 10³ N.

items.stem: On a canted main-line viaduct curve (radius 85 m, bank angle 25 °, μ_s = 0.25), a 1250 kg coach currently travels at 22.9 m s⁻¹. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the upper non-skidding speed limit.
items.workedSolution: At maximum speed, limiting friction μ_s N acts down the slope: N(cos θ − μ_s sin θ) = mg and N(sin θ + μ_s cos θ) = m v_max² / r. Dividing yields v_max = √[g r (sin 25° + 0.25 cos 25°) / (cos 25° − 0.25 sin 25°)] = 26.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves N and down-slope μ_s N horizontally and vertically to obtain v_max = 26.0 m s⁻¹.

items.workedSolution: Because the circular path lies in a horizontal plane, vertical acceleration is zero: N cos θ = mg, so N = (1420 × 9.81) / cos 25° = 1.54 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 25° = mg to obtain N = 1.54 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: A 1580 kg alpine highway tour bus corners at 16.9 m s⁻¹ on a superelevated mountain bend of horizontal radius 58 m banked at 16 °, where the static friction coefficient is 0.4 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). What is the maximum speed at which it can round this banked turn without skidding outward?
items.workedSolution: At maximum speed, limiting friction μ_s N acts down the slope: N(cos θ − μ_s sin θ) = mg and N(sin θ + μ_s cos θ) = m v_max² / r. Dividing yields v_max = √[g r (sin 16° + 0.4 cos 16°) / (cos 16° − 0.4 sin 16°)] = 21.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves N and down-slope μ_s N horizontally and vertically to obtain v_max = 21.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Without relying on lateral tyre or rail grip, a 1950 kg solar-powered cruiser vehicle negotiates a banked desert test circuit of radius 165 m inclined at 16 ° to the horizontal (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find its speed.
items.workedSolution: With zero slope friction, N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = m v² / r. Dividing gives tan θ = v² / (g r), so v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.8 × 165 × tan 16°) = 21.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v = √(g r tan 16°) to obtain 21.5 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Rounding a banked elevated beamway (radius 58 m, bank angle 25 °) with zero lateral friction, a 1580 kg shuttle stays in a horizontal circle. Taking g = 9.81 m s⁻², determine the normal reaction force.
items.workedSolution: Because the circular path lies in a horizontal plane, vertical acceleration is zero: N cos θ = mg, so N = (1580 × 9.81) / cos 25° = 1.71 × 10⁴ N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves vertically N cos 25° = mg to obtain N = 1.71 × 10⁴ N.

items.stem: Without relying on lateral tyre or rail grip, a 1050 kg autonomous mining haul truck negotiates a banked quarry spiral ramp of radius 85 m inclined at 16 ° to the horizontal (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find its speed.
items.workedSolution: With zero slope friction, N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = m v² / r. Dividing gives tan θ = v² / (g r), so v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.8 × 85 × tan 16°) = 15.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v = √(g r tan 16°) to obtain 15.5 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An proving-ground electric sedan of mass 1580 kg rounds a concrete parabolic test banking of horizontal radius 32 m banked at 14 ° to the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². At what design speed is zero lateral friction required along the slope?
items.workedSolution: With zero slope friction, N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = m v² / r. Dividing gives tan θ = v² / (g r), so v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.8 × 32 × tan 14°) = 8.84 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v = √(g r tan 14°) to obtain 8.84 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A 1750 kg alpine highway tour bus corners at 20.8 m s⁻¹ on a superelevated mountain bend of horizontal radius 105 m banked at 16 °, where the static friction coefficient is 0.25 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). What is the maximum speed at which it can round this banked turn without skidding outward?
items.workedSolution: At maximum speed, limiting friction μ_s N acts down the slope: N(cos θ − μ_s sin θ) = mg and N(sin θ + μ_s cos θ) = m v_max² / r. Dividing yields v_max = √[g r (sin 16° + 0.25 cos 16°) / (cos 16° − 0.25 sin 16°)] = 24.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves N and down-slope μ_s N horizontally and vertically to obtain v_max = 24.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Engineers design a superelevated guideway curve with a horizontal curve radius of 85 m and banking angle 28 ° so that a 160 kg carriage corners in a horizontal plane with zero sideways friction (g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical equilibrium N cos 28° = mg gives N = 1.78 × 10³ N. (b) Horizontal component F_c = N sin 28° = 835 N. (c) Setting m v² / r = F_c yields v_ideal = 21.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N cos θ = mg (zero vertical acceleration).
Evaluates F_c = N sin θ or mg tan θ.
Equates m v² / r to F_c and solves for v.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the normal contact force acting on the carriage.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium gives N cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the horizontal centripetal force acting toward the centre of curvature.
workingSteps: Horizontal component of normal reaction provides the centripetal force: F_c = N sin θ = mg tan θ.

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the ideal frictionless cornering speed of the carriage.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = F_c, v = √(F_c r / m) = √(g r tan θ) = 21.1 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: An autonomous mining haul truck of combined mass 880 kg travels around a banked quarry spiral ramp of horizontal radius 58 m inclined at a constant banking angle of 16 ° to the horizontal. At the chosen design speed, zero lateral frictional force acts along the slope. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical equilibrium N cos 16° = mg gives N = 8.97 × 10³ N. (b) Horizontal component F_c = N sin 16° = 2.47 × 10³ N. (c) Setting m v² / r = F_c yields v_ideal = 12.8 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N cos θ = mg (zero vertical acceleration).
Evaluates F_c = N sin θ or mg tan θ.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the normal contact force acting on the shuttle.
workingSteps: Vertical equilibrium gives N cos θ = mg.

parts.prompt: Determine the horizontal centripetal force acting toward the centre of curvature.
workingSteps: Horizontal component of normal reaction provides the centripetal force: F_c = N sin θ = mg tan θ.

parts.prompt: Hence calculate the ideal frictionless cornering speed of the shuttle.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = F_c, v = √(F_c r / m) = √(g r tan θ) = 17.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Orbiting a terrestrial host planet (mass 2.99 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 4.78 × 10⁶ m) at circular orbital radius 7.17 × 10⁶ m, a 280 kg cryogenic infrared space telescope is gravitationally bound. With E_p = 0 at infinity and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate its total mechanical energy.
items.workedSolution: In a circular orbit, E_k = +GMm/(2r) and E_p = −GMm/r, so E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.99 × 10²⁴ × 280) / (2 × 7.17 × 10⁶) = -3.89 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r) with negative sign to obtain -3.89 × 10⁹ J.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits both the negative sign and the virial factor of 1/2, reporting +GMm/r.

items.stem: Above a central rocky exoplanet (mass 7.76 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.1 × 10⁶ m), a 480 kg X-ray timing observatory executes uniform circular motion at altitude h = 3.83 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², find its circular orbital speed.
items.workedSolution: Orbital radius from planet centre r = R_p + h = 5.1 × 10⁶ + 3.83 × 10⁶ = 8.93 × 10⁶ m. Equating GMm / r² = mv² / r gives v = √(GM / r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.76 × 10²⁴ / 8.93 × 10⁶) = 7.61 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Positioned in a circular orbit of radius 1.26 × 10⁷ m around a spherical planetary body of mass 8.36 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.73 × 10⁶ m, a 560 kg magnetospheric plasma observatory prepares a departure burn (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the local escape speed from r = 1.26 × 10⁷ m.
items.workedSolution: Escape from radial distance r requires ½m v_esc² − GMm/r = 0, so v_esc = √(2GM / r) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 8.36 × 10²⁴ / 1.26 × 10⁷) = 9.41 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Mission tracking places a 750 kg ultraviolet spectroscopy satellite at height 7.65 × 10⁶ m above an airless rocky planet of mass 1.01 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.1 × 10⁶ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the orbital period.

items.stem: Comparing circular orbits of radii r₁ = 1.39 × 10⁷ m and r₂ = 4.45 × 10⁷ m around a spherical silicate planet (mass 1.91 × 10²⁵ kg, surface radius 5.57 × 10⁶ m), find the signed change in orbital kinetic energy for a 950 kg laser-interferometry geodesy orbiter raised from r₁ to r₂ (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Because E_k(r) = +GMm/(2r) decreases as r increases, ΔE_k = ½GMm(1/r₂ − 1/r₁) = -2.99 × 10¹⁰ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in E_k = GMm/(2r).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Quotes the final kinetic energy E_k(r₂) rather than the change E_k(r₂) − E_k(r₁).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Reports a positive change +ΔE_k, overlooking that a higher circular orbit has a lower orbital speed and smaller kinetic energy.

items.stem: At orbital radius r = 2.203 × 10⁷ m from the centre of an Earth-mass rocky world (mass 1.73 × 10²⁵ kg, surface radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m), what is the circular orbital speed of a 920 kg ocean-altimetry spacecraft? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Equating GMm / r² = mv² / r gives v = √(GM / r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.73 × 10²⁵ / 2.203 × 10⁷) = 7.24 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 2.203 × 10⁷ m to obtain 7.24 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Determine the escape velocity from orbital radius r = 1.77 × 10⁷ m for a 1100 kg laser-interferometry geodesy orbiter orbiting a spherical silicate planet of mass 2.03 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 4.92 × 10⁶ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Escape from radial distance r requires ½m v_esc² − GMm/r = 0, so v_esc = √(2GM / r) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.03 × 10²⁵ / 1.77 × 10⁷) = 1.24 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates circular orbital speed √(GM / r) and omits the √2 factor needed to escape from orbit.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies circular orbital speed by 2 instead of √2.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates escape speed from the planet's surface R_p rather than from the satellite's orbital radius r.

items.stem: A X-ray timing observatory of mass 1350 kg moves in a circular orbit of radius 3.3 × 10⁷ m around a central rocky exoplanet of mass 2.03 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 7.86 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and zero potential energy at infinity. What is the total mechanical energy of the spacecraft in this orbit?
items.workedSolution: In a circular orbit, E_k = +GMm/(2r) and E_p = −GMm/r, so E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.03 × 10²⁵ × 1350) / (2 × 3.3 × 10⁷) = -2.77 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r) with negative sign to obtain -2.77 × 10¹⁰ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in E_tot = −GMm/(2r), quoting gravitational potential energy −GMm/r instead.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the negative bound-state sign, reporting +GMm/(2r) instead of −GMm/(2r).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits both the negative sign and the virial factor of 1/2, reporting +GMm/r.

items.stem: Thrusters boost a 1500 kg ocean-altimetry spacecraft around an Earth-mass rocky world (mass 4.3 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.54 × 10⁶ m) from a circular orbit of radius 1.21 × 10⁷ m to a higher circular orbit of radius 4.84 × 10⁷ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What minimum mechanical energy must the thrusters supply?

markScheme.criterion: Uses ΔE_tot = ½GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) to obtain 1.33 × 10¹⁰ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reverses initial and final radii, obtaining a negative energy requirement for raising the orbit.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates |E_tot(r₂)| alone instead of subtracting initial total energy E_tot(r₁) from E_tot(r₂).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the gain in gravitational potential energy ΔE_p = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) and forgets the virial reduction in kinetic energy (factor of 1/2).

items.stem: Orbiting a uniform spherical planet (mass 2.27 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 7.54 × 10⁶ m), a 1450 kg planetary gravity-mapping orbiter follows a circular path of orbital radius 3.094 × 10⁷ m measured from the planet's centre (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate its orbital period.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 3.094 × 10⁷ m to obtain 2.78 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: Orbiting a rocky central planet (mass 3.08 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.9 × 10⁶ m) along a circle of radius 8.85 × 10⁶ m, a ion-propelled communications relay has mass 1650 kg. Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate the orbital kinetic energy of the spacecraft.
items.workedSolution: Since m v² / r = G M m / r², orbital kinetic energy is E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r) = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 3.08 × 10²⁴ × 1650) / (2 × 8.85 × 10⁶) = 1.92 × 10¹⁰ J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assigns a negative sign to kinetic energy by confusing E_k with total orbital energy E_tot.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in E_k = ½mv² = GMm/(2r), computing GMm/r instead.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses surface altitude (r − R_p) instead of orbital radius r.

items.stem: Positioned in a circular orbit of radius 1.71 × 10⁷ m around a spherical terrestrial planet of mass 4.61 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 9.51 × 10⁶ m, a 288 kg synthetic-aperture radar satellite prepares a departure burn (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the local escape speed from r = 1.71 × 10⁷ m.
items.workedSolution: Escape from radial distance r requires ½m v_esc² − GMm/r = 0, so v_esc = √(2GM / r) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.61 × 10²⁴ / 1.71 × 10⁷) = 6.00 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates circular orbital speed √(GM / r) and omits the √2 factor needed to escape from orbit.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates escape speed from the planet's surface R_p rather than from the satellite's orbital radius r.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies circular orbital speed by 2 instead of √2.

items.stem: Between circular orbits of radii r₁ = 1.26 × 10⁷ m and r₂ = 2.52 × 10⁷ m around a uniform spherical planet (mass 8.29 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.72 × 10⁶ m), a 463 kg planetary gravity-mapping orbiter coasts along a tangent Hohmann transfer ellipse (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the transit time from periapsis to apoapsis.
items.workedSolution: The transfer ellipse has semi-major axis a = ½(r₁ + r₂) = 1.89 × 10⁷ m. Coasting from periapsis to apoapsis takes half an orbital period: t_H = π√(a³ / GM) = 1.10 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a = ½(r₁ + r₂) and t_H = π√(a³ / GM) to obtain 1.10 × 10⁴ s.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Takes half the outer circular period using r₂ instead of the transfer ellipse semi-major axis (r₁ + r₂)/2.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the full elliptical period 2π√(a³ / GM) instead of the half-orbit Hohmann coast time π√(a³ / GM).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses major axis (r₁ + r₂) instead of semi-major axis a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 in Kepler's third law.

items.stem: Telemetry confirms a 350 kg navigation constellation spacecraft is in a circular orbit of radius 1.131 × 10⁷ m about a spherical host world (mass 6.14 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.54 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Find the circular orbital speed.
items.workedSolution: Equating GMm / r² = mv² / r gives v = √(GM / r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.14 × 10²⁴ / 1.131 × 10⁷) = 6.02 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 1.131 × 10⁷ m to obtain 6.02 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Maintaining a constant surface altitude of 3.94 × 10⁶ m, a 494 kg polar meteorological CubeSat bus circles a charted extrasolar planet (mass 6.14 × 10²⁴ kg, surface radius 5.25 × 10⁶ m). Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², determine its orbital period.
items.workedSolution: Orbital radius from planet centre r = R_p + h = 5.25 × 10⁶ + 3.94 × 10⁶ = 9.19 × 10⁶ m. By Kepler's third law, T = 2π√(r³ / GM) = 2π√((9.19 × 10⁶)³ / (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.14 × 10²⁴)) = 8.65 × 10³ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 9.19 × 10⁶ m to obtain 8.65 × 10³ s.

items.stem: Determine the translational kinetic energy of a 576 kg polar meteorological CubeSat bus in a circular orbit of radius r = 1.32 × 10⁷ m about a charted extrasolar planet (mass 8.6 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.06 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Since m v² / r = G M m / r², orbital kinetic energy is E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r) = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 8.6 × 10²⁴ × 576) / (2 × 1.32 × 10⁷) = 1.25 × 10¹⁰ J.

options.label: A

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 1/2 in E_k = ½mv² = GMm/(2r), computing GMm/r instead.

items.stem: At orbital radius 2.5 × 10⁷ m outside a spherical host world (mass 1.53 × 10²⁵ kg, surface radius 8.08 × 10⁶ m), what threshold speed must a 741 kg navigation constellation spacecraft attain so its total mechanical energy reaches zero? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Escape from radial distance r requires ½m v_esc² − GMm/r = 0, so v_esc = √(2GM / r) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.53 × 10²⁵ / 2.5 × 10⁷) = 9.04 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies circular orbital speed by 2 instead of √2.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates escape speed from the planet's surface R_p rather than from the satellite's orbital radius r.

items.stem: Determine the unpowered coast duration along a Hohmann half-ellipse connecting r₁ = 1.08 × 10⁷ m to r₂ = 3.46 × 10⁷ m for a 978 kg polar meteorological CubeSat bus orbiting a charted extrasolar planet of mass 4.3 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.74 × 10⁶ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: The transfer ellipse has semi-major axis a = ½(r₁ + r₂) = 2.27 × 10⁷ m. Coasting from periapsis to apoapsis takes half an orbital period: t_H = π√(a³ / GM) = 2.01 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a = ½(r₁ + r₂) and t_H = π√(a³ / GM) to obtain 2.01 × 10⁴ s.

items.stem: A synthetic-aperture radar satellite of mass 772 kg travels in a circular orbit at an altitude of 8.1 × 10⁶ m above the surface of a spherical terrestrial planet of mass 1.04 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.4 × 10⁶ m. items.stem: A 339 kg ion-propelled communications relay around a rocky central planet (mass 1.13 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 7.97 × 10⁶ m) executes an elliptical Hohmann transfer with periapsis r₁ = 1.99 × 10⁷ m and apoapsis r₂ = 3.18 × 10⁷ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². How long does the half-ellipse coast from r₁ to r₂ take?
items.workedSolution: The transfer ellipse has semi-major axis a = ½(r₁ + r₂) = 2.59 × 10⁷ m. Coasting from periapsis to apoapsis takes half an orbital period: t_H = π√(a³ / GM) = 1.50 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a = ½(r₁ + r₂) and t_H = π√(a³ / GM) to obtain 1.50 × 10⁴ s.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses major axis (r₁ + r₂) instead of semi-major axis a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 in Kepler's third law.

items.stem: At orbital radius r = 3.186 × 10⁷ m from the centre of a spherical silicate planet (mass 2.34 × 10²⁵ kg, surface radius 7.76 × 10⁶ m), what is the circular orbital speed of a 1490 kg laser-interferometry geodesy orbiter? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 3.186 × 10⁷ m to obtain 7.00 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Orbiting an Earth-mass rocky world (mass 4.74 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.2 × 10⁶ m) at circular orbital radius 9.36 × 10⁶ m, a 1700 kg ocean-altimetry spacecraft is gravitationally bound. With E_p = 0 at infinity and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate its total mechanical energy.
items.workedSolution: In a circular orbit, E_k = +GMm/(2r) and E_p = −GMm/r, so E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.74 × 10²⁴ × 1700) / (2 × 9.36 × 10⁶) = -2.87 × 10¹⁰ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r) with negative sign to obtain -2.87 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: Determine the translational kinetic energy of a 296 kg ultraviolet spectroscopy satellite in a circular orbit of radius r = 1.83 × 10⁷ m about an airless rocky planet (mass 8.84 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 8.3 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Since m v² / r = G M m / r², orbital kinetic energy is E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r) = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 8.84 × 10²⁴ × 296) / (2 × 1.83 × 10⁷) = 4.77 × 10⁹ J.

options.label: A

options.label: C

items.stem: Determine E_k(r₂) − E_k(r₁) when a 635 kg laser-interferometry geodesy orbiter orbiting a spherical silicate planet of mass 2.02 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 6.04 × 10⁶ m transitions from circular radius r₁ = 9.66 × 10⁶ m to r₂ = 2.32 × 10⁷ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Because E_k(r) = +GMm/(2r) decreases as r increases, ΔE_k = ½GMm(1/r₂ − 1/r₁) = -2.58 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.stem: Mission tracking places a 794 kg cryogenic infrared space telescope at height 8.31 × 10⁶ m above a terrestrial host planet of mass 1.39 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.54 × 10⁶ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the circular orbital speed.
items.workedSolution: Orbital radius from planet centre r = R_p + h = 5.54 × 10⁶ + 8.31 × 10⁶ = 1.385 × 10⁷ m. Equating GMm / r² = mv² / r gives v = √(GM / r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.39 × 10²⁵ / 1.385 × 10⁷) = 8.18 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = 1.385 × 10⁷ m to obtain 8.18 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

options.distractorRationale: Substitutes altitude h above the surface instead of total orbital radius r = R_p + h in v = √(GM / r).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Includes an extra factor of √2, calculating escape speed √(2GM / r) instead of circular orbital speed √(GM / r).

options.label: D

items.stem: A 1590 kg planetary gravity-mapping orbiter around a uniform spherical planet (mass 8.76 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.19 × 10⁶ m) executes an elliptical Hohmann transfer with periapsis r₁ = 8.67 × 10⁶ m and apoapsis r₂ = 3.47 × 10⁷ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². How long does the half-ellipse coast from r₁ to r₂ take?
items.workedSolution: The transfer ellipse has semi-major axis a = ½(r₁ + r₂) = 2.17 × 10⁷ m. Coasting from periapsis to apoapsis takes half an orbital period: t_H = π√(a³ / GM) = 1.31 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses a = ½(r₁ + r₂) and t_H = π√(a³ / GM) to obtain 1.31 × 10⁴ s.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Averages the inner and outer half-periods linearly rather than applying T ∝ a^(3/2).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the full elliptical period 2π√(a³ / GM) instead of the half-orbit Hohmann coast time π√(a³ / GM).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses major axis (r₁ + r₂) instead of semi-major axis a = (r₁ + r₂)/2 in Kepler's third law.

items.stem: A synthetic-aperture radar satellite of mass 220 kg orbits a spherical terrestrial planet of mass 3.58 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.1 × 10⁶ m in a circular path at constant altitude 1.79 × 10⁶ m above the surface. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) With orbital radius r = 6.89 × 10⁶ m, g = GM/r² = 5.03 N kg⁻¹. (b) Orbital speed v = √(GM/r) = 5.89 × 10³ m s⁻¹. (c) Period T = 2πr/v = 7.35 × 10³ s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses centre-to-centre orbital radius r in g = GM / r².
Applies T = 2πr / v or Kepler's third law.

items.stem: A autonomous orbital servicing tug of mass 320 kg initially orbits a dense terrestrial world (mass 4.18 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) in a circular orbit of radius r₁ = 7.57 × 10⁶ m. Propulsion burns transfer it into a higher coaxial circular orbit of radius r₂ = 1.21 × 10⁷ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Initial bound energy E_tot(r₁) = −GMm/(2r₁) = -5.89 × 10⁹ J. (b) Final bound energy E_tot(r₂) = -3.69 × 10⁹ J, so ΔE_tot = 2.21 × 10⁹ J. (c) Outer orbital period T₂ = 2π√(r₂³/GM) = 1.58 × 10⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Kepler's third law at outer radius r₂.

parts.prompt: Calculate the initial total mechanical energy of the autonomous orbital servicing tug in the orbit of radius r₁.
Determine the minimum mechanical energy that must be supplied to transfer the autonomous orbital servicing tug into the circular orbit of radius r₂.
Calculate the orbital period of the autonomous orbital servicing tug in the outer circular orbit of radius r₂.

items.stem: In a circular orbit of centre-to-centre radius 1.38 × 10⁷ m around a uniform spherical planet (mass 4.48 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.64 × 10⁶ m), a 420 kg planetary gravity-mapping orbiter has E_p = 0 at infinity. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) E_k = GMm/(2r) = 4.55 × 10⁹ J. (b) E_p = −GMm/r = -9.09 × 10⁹ J. (c) Total mechanical energy E_tot = E_k + E_p = −GMm/(2r) = -4.55 × 10⁹ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_p = −GMm / r including negative sign.
Sums E_k + E_p or applies E_tot = −GMm / (2r).

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy of the planetary gravity-mapping orbiter in this circular orbit.
workingSteps: From m v² / r = G M m / r², E_k = ½ m v² = G M m / (2r).

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the planetary gravity-mapping orbiter.
Determine the total mechanical energy of the planetary gravity-mapping orbiter.
workingSteps: E_tot = E_k + E_p = −G M m / (2r) = -4.55 × 10⁹ J.

items.stem: A conical pendulum (0.6 kg, cord length 2.75 m) in an undergraduate mechanics laboratory revolves steadily with its cord inclined at 42 ° to the vertical (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Calculate the horizontal acceleration toward the centre of the circle.
items.workedSolution: Dividing horizontal Newton's second law T sin θ = m a_c by vertical equilibrium T cos θ = mg gives a_c = g tan θ = 9.81 × tan 42° = 8.83 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = g tan 42° to obtain 8.83 m s⁻².

items.stem: Swinging steadily around a vertical axis in an overhead cable rig, a 0.85 kg suspended ice-arena tracking camera pod hangs from a 1.4 m tether inclined at 42 ° to the vertical (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is its speed along the circular path?
items.workedSolution: Orbit radius r = L sin θ = 1.4 sin 42° = 0.937 m. Since T sin θ = mv²/r and T cos θ = mg, v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.81 × 0.937 × tan 42°) = 2.88 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = L sin θ and v = √(g L sin θ tan θ) to obtain 2.88 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A 1.2 kg wind-tunnel tethered aerodynamic probe attached to a 2.1 m light wire revolves in a horizontal circle inside a rotary calibration fixture at a constant semi-vertical angle of 24 °. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the time period of one complete revolution?
items.workedSolution: From T cos θ = mg and T sin θ = m ω² (L sin θ), ω = √(g / (L cos θ)). Thus the period is P = 2π√(L cos θ / g) = 2π√((2.1 cos 24°) / 9.8) = 2.78 s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2π√(L cos 24° / g) to obtain 2.78 s.

items.stem: During rotational testing in an inertial navigation testbed, a 2.2 kg reference mass on a 0.65 m tether describes a horizontal circle with the tether inclined at 20 ° to the downward vertical. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², calculate the tension force in the tether.
items.workedSolution: Vertical equilibrium requires T cos θ = mg, so T = (2.2 × 9.8) / cos 20° = 22.9 N.

items.stem: A conical pendulum in a frictionless swivel mast consists of a 2.5 kg steel sphere and a 1.4 m inextensible string making 38 ° with the vertical axis (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Determine the orbital speed of the steel sphere.
items.workedSolution: Orbit radius r = L sin θ = 1.4 sin 38° = 0.862 m. Since T sin θ = mv²/r and T cos θ = mg, v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.81 × 0.862 × tan 38°) = 2.57 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = L sin θ and v = √(g L sin θ tan θ) to obtain 2.57 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Suspended by a 2.75 m line in a rigid ceiling pivot, a 2.5 kg weight executes uniform horizontal circular motion at 42 ° to the vertical (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Select the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration.
items.workedSolution: Dividing horizontal Newton's second law T sin θ = m a_c by vertical equilibrium T cos θ = mg gives a_c = g tan θ = 9.81 × tan 42° = 8.83 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = g tan 42° to obtain 8.83 m s⁻².

items.stem: Inside a fairground swing carousel, a 1.1 m suspension wire supports a 4.5 kg gondola whirling at a steady semi-vertical cone angle of 38 ° (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Calculate the tangential speed of the gondola.
items.workedSolution: Orbit radius r = L sin θ = 1.1 sin 38° = 0.677 m. Since T sin θ = mv²/r and T cos θ = mg, v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.81 × 0.677 × tan 38°) = 2.28 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = L sin θ and v = √(g L sin θ tan θ) to obtain 2.28 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: How long does one full horizontal orbit take for a 0.45 kg sphere suspended on a 2.1 m tether inclined at 20 ° to the vertical in a guidance-sensor test chamber? Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: From T cos θ = mg and T sin θ = m ω² (L sin θ), ω = √(g / (L cos θ)). Thus the period is P = 2π√(L cos θ / g) = 2π√((2.1 cos 20°) / 9.8) = 2.82 s.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates 2π√(L cos 20° / g) to obtain 2.82 s.

items.stem: Engineers operating a steam-turbine speed regulator spin a 0.75 kg governor mass suspended by a 0.95 m wire so that the wire makes a steady 24 ° angle with the vertical axis (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find the tension supported by the wire.
items.workedSolution: Vertical equilibrium requires T cos θ = mg, so T = (0.75 × 9.8) / cos 24° = 8.05 N.

markScheme.criterion: Resolves T cos 24° = mg to obtain T = 8.05 N.

items.stem: A conical pendulum in a frictionless swivel mast consists of a 1.8 kg steel sphere and a 1.25 m inextensible string making 42 ° with the vertical axis (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Determine the orbital speed of the steel sphere.
items.workedSolution: Orbit radius r = L sin θ = 1.25 sin 42° = 0.836 m. Since T sin θ = mv²/r and T cos θ = mg, v = √(g r tan θ) = √(9.81 × 0.836 × tan 42°) = 2.72 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses r = L sin θ and v = √(g L sin θ tan θ) to obtain 2.72 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A 2.4 m tether in a steady slewing test guides a 0.85 kg ballast block around a horizontal circle at a steady cone half-angle of 38 ° (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). Find the inward radial acceleration of the ballast block.
items.workedSolution: Dividing horizontal Newton's second law T sin θ = m a_c by vertical equilibrium T cos θ = mg gives a_c = g tan θ = 9.81 × tan 38° = 7.66 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies a_c = g tan 38° to obtain 7.66 m s⁻².

items.stem: Engineers testing rotational instrumentation in a rotary calibration fixture whirl a 1.2 kg probe on the end of a 2.1 m tether. Throughout the motion, the tether makes a constant semi-vertical angle of 20 ° with the vertical axis. Use g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical equilibrium T cos 20° = (1.2)(9.8) gives T = 12.5 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 2.1 sin 20° = 0.718 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 1.60 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 2.82 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).

items.stem: In an inertial navigation testbed, a gyroscopic reference mass of mass 1.4 kg is suspended from a fixed ceiling pivot by a light inextensible cord of length 0.8 m. The reference mass moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle such that the cord maintains a steady angle of 20 ° to the vertical. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical equilibrium T cos 20° = (1.4)(9.8) gives T = 14.6 N. (b) Horizontal radius r = 0.8 sin 20° = 0.274 m; horizontal dynamics T sin θ = mv²/r yields v = 0.988 m s⁻¹. (c) Period P = 2πr / v = 1.74 s.

markScheme.criterion: Equates vertical component T cos θ to weight mg.
Uses r = L sin θ and equates T sin θ (or mg tan θ) to m v² / r.
Applies P = 2π r / v or P = 2π√(L cos θ / g).

items.stem: Determine the low-redshift recession speed (in km s⁻¹) of a lenticular field galaxy whose neutral Sodium D absorption doublet shifts from 589 nm to 626.7 nm. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and H₀ = 73.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: z = Δλ / λ₀ = (626.7 − 589) / 589 = 0.0640. In the low-redshift regime, v ≈ z c = 0.0640 × 3.00 × 10⁵ km s⁻¹ = 1.92 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses v ≈ (Δλ / λ₀) c to obtain 1.92 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹.

items.stem: Determine the redshifted wavelength (in nm) received at Earth for the Magnesium b triplet feature (rest wavelength 517.5 nm) emitted by a giant cD cluster-centre galaxy at distance 75.57 Mpc, taking H₀ = 71.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: Recession speed v = H₀ d = 71.5 × 75.57 = 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹. Redshift z = v / c = 0.0180, so λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 517.5 × (1 + 0.0180) = 527 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v = H₀d, z = v/c, and λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 527 nm.

items.stem: When photons of the singly ionized Oxygen doublet (λ₀ = 372.7 nm) left a blue emission-line galaxy, the universe had scale factor R; today (scale factor R₀, H₀ = 69.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹) those photons arrive at 596.32 nm. Determine R / R₀.
items.workedSolution: Since 1 + z = R₀ / R = λ_obs / λ₀, the emission-to-present scale-factor ratio is R / R₀ = λ₀ / λ_obs = 372.7 / 596.32 = 0.625.

items.stem: In the spectrum of a star-forming barred spiral galaxy (surveyed with H₀ = 67.4 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹), the Hydrogen-beta Balmer emission line of rest wavelength 486.1 nm is measured at 494.85 nm. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the recession speed of the galaxy in km s⁻¹?

items.stem: In an extragalactic survey with H₀ = 72 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, the neutral Helium spectral line (rest wavelength 587.6 nm) from a isolated ring galaxy arrives at 598.18 nm. Taking c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, calculate the Hubble distance in Mpc.
items.workedSolution: Redshift z = (λ_obs − λ₀) / λ₀ = (598.18 − 587.6) / 587.6 = 0.0180. Recession speed v ≈ z c = 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹. From Hubble's law v = H₀ d, d = v / H₀ = 5.40 × 10³ / 72 = 75.0 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Finds z = 0.0180, v = 5.40 × 10³ km s⁻¹, and d = v / H₀ = 75.0 Mpc.

markScheme.criterion: Finds z = 0.0640, v = 1.92 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹, and d = v / H₀ = 291 Mpc.

items.stem: Situated 75.78 Mpc from Earth, a lenticular field galaxy recedes according to Hubble's law with H₀ = 74 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). Predict the observed wavelength in nm of its neutral Sodium D absorption doublet (λ₀ = 589 nm).

items.stem: Spectroscopy of a giant cD cluster-centre galaxy detects the Magnesium b triplet feature shifted from its rest value 517.5 nm to 651.53 nm (H₀ = 72 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹). Calculate the emission-to-present cosmic scale-factor ratio R / R₀.
items.workedSolution: Since 1 + z = R₀ / R = λ_obs / λ₀, the emission-to-present scale-factor ratio is R / R₀ = λ₀ / λ_obs = 517.5 / 651.53 = 0.794.

items.stem: Using Hubble constant H₀ = 68 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, find the observed wavelength in nm of the Hydrogen-beta Balmer emission line (λ₀ = 486.1 nm) from a star-forming barred spiral galaxy located 293 Mpc away.
items.workedSolution: Recession speed v = H₀ d = 68 × 293 = 1.99 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹. Redshift z = v / c = 0.0664, so λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 486.1 × (1 + 0.0664) = 518 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v = H₀d, z = v/c, and λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 518 nm.

items.stem: When photons of the neutral Helium spectral line (λ₀ = 587.6 nm) left a isolated ring galaxy, the universe had scale factor R; today (scale factor R₀, H₀ = 73.5 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹) those photons arrive at 966.01 nm. Determine R / R₀.
items.workedSolution: Since 1 + z = R₀ / R = λ_obs / λ₀, the emission-to-present scale-factor ratio is R / R₀ = λ₀ / λ_obs = 587.6 / 966.01 = 0.608.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v = H₀d, z = v/c, and λ_obs = λ₀(1 + z) = 495 nm.

items.stem: Engineers test a 480 kg autonomous warehouse transport robot cruising at 12.4 m s⁻¹ on a flat epoxy distribution floor of radius 52 m with μ_s = 0.74 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Calculate the limiting non-skidding speed on this bend.
items.workedSolution: At the verge of skidding, m v_max² / r = μ_s m g, independent of mass: v_max = √(μ_s g r) = √(0.74 × 9.8 × 52) = 19.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 19.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Safety engineers specify an unbanked wet-asphalt roundabout of radius 90 m for a 760 kg proving-ground test saloon travelling at 13.5 m s⁻¹. Using g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the minimum static friction coefficient needed.
items.workedSolution: No-skid cornering requires μ_s m g ≥ m v² / r, so μ_min = v² / (g r) = (13.5)² / (9.81 × 90) = 0.206.

items.stem: A competition sprint kart of mass 1320 kg negotiates a flat hairpin bend of radius 105 m at a constant speed of 13.8 m s⁻¹ without skidding. The coefficient of static friction between its rubber tyres and the surface is 0.55 (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What lateral frictional force acts on the rubber tyres?
items.workedSolution: Because 13.8 m s⁻¹ is below the skidding threshold v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 23.8 m s⁻¹, static friction self-adjusts to match the required centripetal force: f_s = m v² / r = 1320 × (13.8)² / 105 = 2.39 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f_s = m v² / r (not μ_s mg) to obtain 2.39 × 10³ N.

items.stem: Telemetry from a 1650 kg short-track speed-skating sled cornering without slip on a flat synthetic training ring (radius 105 m, μ_s = 0.36) records a speed of 14.6 m s⁻¹. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the static frictional force exerted by the ground.
items.workedSolution: Because 14.6 m s⁻¹ is below the skidding threshold v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 19.2 m s⁻¹, static friction self-adjusts to match the required centripetal force: f_s = m v² / r = 1650 × (14.6)² / 105 = 3.35 × 10³ N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f_s = m v² / r (not μ_s mg) to obtain 3.35 × 10³ N.

items.stem: A 140 kg heavy-duty rescue ambulance circles a flat coastal highway curve of radius 28 m at 11.7 m s⁻¹. If μ_s = 0.74 and g = 9.81 m s⁻², what critical speed marks the onset of skidding?
items.workedSolution: At the verge of skidding, m v_max² / r = μ_s m g, independent of mass: v_max = √(μ_s g r) = √(0.74 × 9.81 × 28) = 14.3 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 14.3 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A Formula-Student electric race car of mass 220 kg negotiates a level dry-tarmac skidpad of radius 90 m at a constant speed of 14.8 m s⁻¹ without skidding. The coefficient of static friction between its slick tyres and the surface is 0.74 (g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What lateral frictional force acts on the slick tyres?
items.workedSolution: Because 14.8 m s⁻¹ is below the skidding threshold v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 25.6 m s⁻¹, static friction self-adjusts to match the required centripetal force: f_s = m v² / r = 220 × (14.8)² / 90 = 535 N.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f_s = m v² / r (not μ_s mg) to obtain 535 N.

items.stem: Safety engineers specify an unbanked wet-asphalt roundabout of radius 35 m for a 920 kg proving-ground test saloon travelling at 12.2 m s⁻¹. Using g = 9.81 m s⁻², calculate the minimum static friction coefficient needed.
items.workedSolution: No-skid cornering requires μ_s m g ≥ m v² / r, so μ_min = v² / (g r) = (12.2)² / (9.81 × 35) = 0.433.

items.stem: Engineers test a 1650 kg urban light-rail maintenance bogie cruising at 16.4 m s⁻¹ on a horizontal depot loop of radius 90 m with μ_s = 0.74 (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Calculate the limiting non-skidding speed on this bend.
items.workedSolution: At the verge of skidding, m v_max² / r = μ_s m g, independent of mass: v_max = √(μ_s g r) = √(0.74 × 9.8 × 90) = 25.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 25.5 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A Formula-Student electric race car of mass 140 kg travels at a constant speed of 6.23 m s⁻¹ along a level dry-tarmac skidpad of radius 28 m. The coefficient of static friction between its slick tyres and the ground is 0.42. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a_c = v² / r = (6.23)² / 28 = 1.39 m s⁻². (b) Below the skid limit, f_s = m a_c = 140 × 1.39 = 194 N. (c) Maximum non-skidding speed v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 10.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.

workingSteps: Since the track-cycling sprinter does not skid, static friction supplies the required centripetal force.

parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum speed at which the track-cycling sprinter can negotiate this curve without skidding.
workingSteps: At the skid limit, m v_max² / r = μ_s m g.

items.stem: The top-view diagram shows a 1480 kg competition sprint kart rounding a flat hairpin bend of radius 65 m at a steady speed of 8.79 m s⁻¹. Between the rubber tyres and the surface, μ_s = 0.36. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².
items.workedSolution: (a) a_c = v² / r = (8.79)² / 65 = 1.19 m s⁻². (b) Below the skid limit, f_s = m a_c = 1480 × 1.19 = 1.76 × 10³ N. (c) Maximum non-skidding speed v_max = √(μ_s g r) = 15.2 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies mass by centripetal acceleration (rather than using limiting μ_s mg).
Equates m v_max² / r to μ_s mg.

items.stem: Determine the stellar radius of Star Alpha as a multiple of R☉ given its HR coordinates from an open-cluster Gaia photometric survey: T = 3800 K and L = 180 L☉. Use L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 180 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 6.89 × 10²⁸ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 2.15 × 10¹⁰ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 31.0 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 31.0 R☉.

items.stem: In a wide-field optical sky survey, Star Gamma is plotted on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram at surface temperature 8400 K and luminosity 24 L☉. Take L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What is the radius of Star Gamma in solar radii (R☉)?
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 24 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 9.19 × 10²⁷ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 1.61 × 10⁹ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 2.31 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 2.31 R☉.

items.stem: Photometry in a space-astrometry cluster catalogue locates Star Epsilon at effective temperature 6600 K and luminosity 4.5 L☉ on the Hertzsprung–Russell chart. Taking L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, find its radius in R☉.
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 4.5 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.72 × 10²⁷ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 1.13 × 10⁹ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 1.62 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 1.62 R☉.

items.stem: Determine the stellar radius of Star Zeta as a multiple of R☉ given its HR coordinates from an interferometric stellar benchmark sample: T = 4100 K and L = 260 L☉. Use L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 260 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 9.96 × 10²⁸ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 2.22 × 10¹⁰ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 32.0 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 32.0 R☉.

items.stem: On the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram compiled from a galactic-disc multi-band stellar census (with evolutionary region labels masked), Star Theta has effective surface temperature 9200 K and luminosity 48000 L☉. In which stellar evolutionary region does Star Theta lie?
items.workedSolution: With T = 9200 K and L = 48000 L☉ (note temperature increases from right to left on an HR diagram), Star Theta lies in the supergiant region (supergiant).

markScheme.criterion: Identifies the supergiant region from T = 9200 K and L = 48000 L☉.

items.stem: In a globular-cluster stellar population chart, Star Iota is plotted on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram at surface temperature 7600 K and luminosity 14 L☉. Take L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What is the radius of Star Iota in solar radii (R☉)?
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 14 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 5.36 × 10²⁷ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 1.50 × 10⁹ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 2.16 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 2.16 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 46.0 R☉.

items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 188 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 7.20 × 10²⁸ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 2.14 × 10¹⁰ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 30.8 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 30.8 R☉.

items.stem: On the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram compiled from an interferometric stellar benchmark sample (with evolutionary region labels masked), Star Delta-2 has effective surface temperature 4460 K and luminosity 36600 L☉. In which stellar evolutionary region does Star Delta-2 lie?
items.workedSolution: With T = 4460 K and L = 36600 L☉ (note temperature increases from right to left on an HR diagram), Star Delta-2 lies in the supergiant region (supergiant).

markScheme.criterion: Identifies the supergiant region from T = 4460 K and L = 36600 L☉.

items.stem: On the HR diagram derived from a galactic-disc multi-band stellar census, Star Zeta-2 has photospheric temperature 4160 K and bolometric luminosity 272 L☉ (L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴). Calculate R / R☉ for Star Zeta-2.
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 272 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.04 × 10²⁹ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 2.21 × 10¹⁰ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 31.7 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 31.7 R☉.

items.stem: Photometry in an open-cluster Gaia photometric survey locates Star Iota-2 at effective temperature 7710 K and luminosity 14.6 L☉ on the Hertzsprung–Russell chart. Taking L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, find its radius in R☉.
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 14.6 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 5.59 × 10²⁷ W. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 1.49 × 10⁹ m, so R / R☉ = R / (6.96 × 10⁸) = 2.14 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Stefan-Boltzmann scaling to obtain 2.14 R☉.

items.stem: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram from a southern-hemisphere spectroscopic star survey plots four stars with region names masked. Star Beta has surface temperature 15000 K and luminosity 0.004 L☉. Take L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) Star Beta lies in the white-dwarf region. (b) L = 0.004 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.53 × 10²⁴ W. (c) R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 6.52 × 10⁶ m = 0.00936 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] and divides by R☉.

parts.prompt: Calculate the luminosity of Star Beta in watts.
Determine the radius of Star Beta as a multiple of the solar radius R☉.

items.stem: Compiled during a deep-sky echelle spectrograph programme, an unlabelled Hertzsprung–Russell chart includes Star Delta at effective temperature 4400 K and bolometric luminosity 35000 L☉ (L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴).
items.workedSolution: (a) Star Delta lies in the supergiant region. (b) L = 35000 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.34 × 10³¹ W. (c) R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 2.24 × 10¹¹ m = 322 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] and divides by R☉.

items.stem: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram from an orbital observatory HR calibration field plots four stars with region names masked. Star Theta-2 has surface temperature 9330 K and luminosity 50200 L☉. Take L☉ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, R☉ = 6.96 × 10⁸ m, and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) Star Theta-2 lies in the supergiant region. (b) L = 50200 × 3.83 × 10²⁶ = 1.92 × 10³¹ W. (c) R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 5.97 × 10¹⁰ m = 85.7 R☉.

markScheme.criterion: Applies R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] and divides by R☉.

items.stem: A radial drill shaft inside a uniform spherical basaltic terrestrial planetoid (total mass 2.69 × 10²⁵ kg, surface radius 4.92 × 10⁶ m) stations a 123 kg orbital transponder at r = 3.2 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², determine g(r).
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.69 × 10²⁵ × 3.2 × 10⁶) / (4.92 × 10⁶)³ = 48.2 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 3.2 × 10⁶ m to obtain 48.2 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A radial drill shaft inside a uniform spherical cratered terrestrial dwarf planet (total mass 4.78 × 10²⁴ kg, surface radius 1.18 × 10⁷ m) stations a 250 kg polar radar surveyor at r = 6.49 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², determine g(r).
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.78 × 10²⁴ × 6.49 × 10⁶) / (1.18 × 10⁷)³ = 1.26 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Model a charted extrasolar rocky world as a sphere of uniform density with total mass 3.38 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 5.9 × 10⁶ m. A magnetospheric probe of mass 370 kg descends along a radial borehole to distance 2.36 × 10⁶ m from the planet's centre. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational field strength at this interior point?
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 3.38 × 10²⁴ × 2.36 × 10⁶) / (5.9 × 10⁶)³ = 2.59 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 2.36 × 10⁶ m to obtain 2.59 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Inside a uniform-density tidally locked silicate exoplanet (mass 1.25 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 3.5 × 10⁶ m), a 650 kg descent lander reaches radial distance 8.75 × 10⁵ m from the planetary centre (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the local gravitational field strength.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.25 × 10²⁵ × 8.75 × 10⁵) / (3.5 × 10⁶)³ = 17.0 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 8.75 × 10⁵ m to obtain 17.0 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A deep-shaft gravimeter of mass 900 kg is located at radial distance 2.43 × 10⁷ m from the centre of an airless synthetic uniform planetary body of mass 2.63 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and potential to be zero at infinity, what is the gravitational potential at the deep-shaft gravimeter's position?
items.workedSolution: Outside the spherical mass, V_g = −G M / r = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.63 × 10²⁵) / 2.43 × 10⁷ = -7.22 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes V_g = −GM / r = -7.22 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ including the negative sign.

items.stem: Determine the scalar gravitational potential V_g (relative to zero at infinity) at a 360 kg subsurface borehole sensor positioned 1.51 × 10⁷ m from the centre of a uniform-density silicate moon of mass 1.53 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 7.21 × 10⁶ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Outside the spherical mass, V_g = −G M / r = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.53 × 10²⁴) / 1.51 × 10⁷ = -6.76 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes V_g = −GM / r = -6.76 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ including the negative sign.

items.stem: Assuming uniform internal density throughout a spherical cratered terrestrial dwarf planet of mass 9.83 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 7.54 × 10⁶ m, find the gravitational field strength experienced by a 844 kg polar radar surveyor at interior radius 5.66 × 10⁶ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 9.83 × 10²⁴ × 5.66 × 10⁶) / (7.54 × 10⁶)³ = 8.66 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 5.66 × 10⁶ m to obtain 8.66 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A radial drill shaft inside a uniform spherical charted extrasolar rocky world (total mass 7.58 × 10²⁴ kg, surface radius 1.08 × 10⁷ m) stations a 1010 kg magnetospheric probe at r = 7.02 × 10⁶ m from the centre. Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², determine g(r).
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.58 × 10²⁴ × 7.02 × 10⁶) / (1.08 × 10⁷)³ = 2.82 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 7.02 × 10⁶ m to obtain 2.82 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A cryobot instrument package of mass 803 kg is located at radial distance 3.24 × 10⁷ m from the centre of an airless icy outer-system dwarf world of mass 6.76 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 8.52 × 10⁶ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and potential to be zero at infinity, what is the gravitational potential at the cryobot instrument package's position?
items.workedSolution: Outside the spherical mass, V_g = −G M / r = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.76 × 10²⁴) / 3.24 × 10⁷ = -1.39 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes V_g = −GM / r = -1.39 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ including the negative sign.

items.stem: Model a tidally locked silicate exoplanet as a sphere of uniform density with total mass 2.21 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 7.76 × 10⁶ m. A descent lander of mass 190 kg descends along a radial borehole to distance 4.27 × 10⁶ m from the planet's centre. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational field strength at this interior point?
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.21 × 10²⁵ × 4.27 × 10⁶) / (7.76 × 10⁶)³ = 13.5 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 4.27 × 10⁶ m to obtain 13.5 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Assuming uniform internal density throughout a spherical charted extrasolar rocky world of mass 1.82 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 6.39 × 10⁶ m, find the gravitational field strength experienced by a 402 kg magnetospheric probe at interior radius 1.6 × 10⁶ m (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.82 × 10²⁵ × 1.6 × 10⁶) / (6.39 × 10⁶)³ = 7.44 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 1.6 × 10⁶ m to obtain 7.44 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Inside a uniform-density basaltic terrestrial planetoid (mass 7.78 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 3.91 × 10⁶ m), a 134 kg orbital transponder reaches radial distance 2.15 × 10⁶ m from the planetary centre (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the local gravitational field strength.

items.stem: Determine the surface escape velocity for an unpowered projectile launched from a spherical charted extrasolar rocky world of mass 3.81 × 10²⁵ kg and radius 3.38 × 10⁶ m, given an exterior 370 kg magnetospheric probe at r = 7.1 × 10⁶ m and G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
items.workedSolution: Setting ½m v_esc² − G M m / R = 0 gives v_esc = √(2 G M / R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 3.81 × 10²⁵ / 3.38 × 10⁶) = 3.88 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates surface escape speed √(2GM / R) = 3.88 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Inside a uniform-density cratered terrestrial dwarf planet (mass 2.27 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 1.46 × 10⁷ m), a 272 kg polar radar surveyor reaches radial distance 5.84 × 10⁶ m from the planetary centre (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). Calculate the local gravitational field strength.
items.workedSolution: Inside a uniform sphere (r < R), enclosed mass M_enc = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = G M r / R³ = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.27 × 10²⁵ × 5.84 × 10⁶) / (1.46 × 10⁷)³ = 2.84 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gravitational field strength at r = 5.84 × 10⁶ m to obtain 2.84 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: A spherical basaltic terrestrial planetoid (mass 2.85 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 4.72 × 10⁶ m) is observed by a 825 kg orbital transponder at radial distance 1.79 × 10⁷ m. Taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², at what minimum speed must an object leave the surface R to reach infinity?
items.workedSolution: Setting ½m v_esc² − G M m / R = 0 gives v_esc = √(2 G M / R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 2.85 × 10²⁴ / 4.72 × 10⁶) = 8.97 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates surface escape speed √(2GM / R) = 8.97 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A blue-white main-sequence star Vega-analog with total luminosity 1.46 × 10²⁹ W shows an annual parallax angle of 0.15 arcsec over a 1 AU baseline in an orbital bolometric photometer (1 pc is the distance at which a 1 AU baseline subtends a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec)). Using 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, calculate its apparent brightness received at Earth.
items.workedSolution: d = (1 / 0.15) pc = 6.67 pc = 2.06 × 10¹⁷ m. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 1.46 × 10²⁹ / (4π × (2.06 × 10¹⁷)²) = 2.75 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = (1/p) pc to metres and evaluates b = L/(4πd²) = 2.75 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

items.stem: Determine the distance in light-years to a solar-type G-dwarf exoplanet host (luminosity 1.46 × 10³⁰ W) whose annual parallax angle across a 1 AU baseline is 0.22 arcsec in a transit-photometry telescope (1 pc is the distance at which a 1 AU baseline subtends a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec)). Take 1 pc = 3.26 ly.
items.workedSolution: Distance in parsecs d = 1 / p = 1 / 0.22 = 4.55 pc. Converting to light-years gives d = 4.55 × 3.26 = 14.8 ly.

items.stem: Given bolometric luminosity L = 3.14 × 10²⁹ W and observed brightness b = 2.687 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻² in a cooled CCD radiometer (1 AU baseline) (1 pc is the distance at which a 1 AU baseline subtends a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec)), find the stellar parallax angle in arcseconds (take 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m).
items.workedSolution: From b = L / (4π d²), d = √[L / (4π b)] = 9.64 × 10¹⁶ m = 3.13 pc. Hence p = 1 / d_pc = 0.320 arcsec.

markScheme.criterion: Solves d = √[L/(4πb)] in parsecs and p = 1/d = 0.320 arcsec.

items.stem: Astrometric measurements from a stellar intensity interferometer over a 1 AU orbital baseline determine that a bright southern-sky reference star (luminosity 9.96 × 10²⁹ W) has an annual parallax angle of 0.38 arcsec (1 pc is the distance at which a 1 AU baseline subtends a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec)). Take 1 pc = 3.26 ly. What is the distance to the star in light-years?
items.workedSolution: Distance in parsecs d = 1 / p = 1 / 0.38 = 2.63 pc. Converting to light-years gives d = 2.63 × 3.26 = 8.58 ly.

items.stem: A calibrated cool K-type giant Aldebaran-analog of known luminosity 2.14 × 10²⁹ W produces apparent brightness 5.609 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻² at an infrared space observatory across a 1 AU orbital baseline (1 pc is the distance at which a 1 AU baseline subtends a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec)). Using 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, calculate its expected parallax angle in arcseconds.
items.workedSolution: From b = L / (4π d²), d = √[L / (4π b)] = 5.51 × 10¹⁶ m = 1.79 pc. Hence p = 1 / d_pc = 0.560 arcsec.

markScheme.criterion: Solves d = √[L/(4πb)] in parsecs and p = 1/d = 0.560 arcsec.

markScheme.criterion: Solves d = √[L/(4πb)] in parsecs and p = 1/d = 0.153 arcsec.

items.stem: Six-month baseline observations (1 AU radius) with a stellar intensity interferometer yield parallax p = 0.571 arcsec for a bright southern-sky reference star radiating 2.21 × 10²⁹ W (1 pc is the distance at which a 1 AU baseline subtends a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec)). Given 1 pc = 3.26 ly, how many light-years away is the star?
items.workedSolution: Distance in parsecs d = 1 / p = 1 / 0.571 = 1.75 pc. Converting to light-years gives d = 1.75 × 3.26 = 5.71 ly.

items.stem: From a high-altitude observatory, a yellow-white standard-candle star has bolometric output 7.1 × 10²⁹ W and annual parallax p = 0.693 arcsec on a 1 AU baseline (1 pc is the distance at which a 1 AU baseline subtends a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec)). Taking 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, find the radiant flux density arriving at Earth.
items.workedSolution: d = (1 / 0.693) pc = 1.44 pc = 4.45 × 10¹⁶ m. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 7.1 × 10²⁹ / (4π × (4.45 × 10¹⁶)²) = 2.85 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Converts d = (1/p) pc to metres and evaluates b = L/(4πd²) = 2.85 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

items.stem: Using a 1 AU orbital baseline, an optical interferometry array measures an annual parallax angle of 0.18 arcsec for a eclipsing-binary primary component of total luminosity 4.6 × 10²⁹ W (1 pc is the distance at which a 1 AU baseline subtends a parallax angle of 1 arcsecond, so d / pc = 1 / (p / arcsec)). Take 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m.
items.workedSolution: (a) d = 1 / 0.18 = 5.56 pc. (b) In SI units, d = 1.71 × 10¹⁷ m. (c) Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = 1.25 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies distance in parsecs by 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m pc⁻¹.
Applies inverse-square law b = L / (4π d²).

items.stem: A spherical blackbody hot B-type Orion-association star catalogued by an ultraviolet sky survey radiates total power 2.38 × 10²⁸ W with spectral peak λ_max = 580 nm (b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴). Calculate its stellar radius.
items.workedSolution: By Wien's law, T = b / λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (580 × 10⁻⁹) = 5.00 × 10³ K. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 7.31 × 10⁹ m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds T = 5.00 × 10³ K via Wien's law and R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 7.31 × 10⁹ m.

items.stem: Determine the radiant flux density b = L / (4πd²) received at a space-based spectrometer from a spherical blackbody luminous F-type subgiant of radius 3.83 × 10⁹ m and surface temperature 5800 K located 4.38 × 10¹⁶ m away (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴).
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 4π R² σ T⁴ = 4π(3.83 × 10⁹)²(5.67 × 10⁻⁸)(5800)⁴ = 1.18 × 10²⁸ W. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = σ T⁴ (R / d)² = 4.91 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = 4πR²σT⁴ and b = L / (4πd²) to obtain 4.91 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

items.stem: Observations by a wide-field photometric survey yield bolometric luminosity L = 5.81 × 10²⁸ W and Wien peak wavelength 464 nm for a spherical blackbody metal-poor halo giant star. Taking b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, find R.
items.workedSolution: By Wien's law, T = b / λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (464 × 10⁻⁹) = 6.25 × 10³ K. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 7.31 × 10⁹ m.

options.distractorRationale: Omits the spherical area factor 4π in L = 4π R² σ T⁴ when solving for stellar radius R.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses T² instead of T⁴ in the Stefan-Boltzmann law.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates R² = L / (4π σ T⁴) and forgets to take the square root.

items.stem: Observations with a high-altitude observatory target a spherical blackbody yellow-white standard-candle star of radius 3.83 × 10⁹ m and effective surface temperature 8000 K situated 2.41 × 10¹⁶ m from the detector. Take σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What apparent brightness (radiant intensity) arrives at the detector?
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 4π R² σ T⁴ = 4π(3.83 × 10⁹)²(5.67 × 10⁻⁸)(8000)⁴ = 4.28 × 10²⁸ W. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = σ T⁴ (R / d)² = 5.87 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = 4πR²σT⁴ and b = L / (4πd²) to obtain 5.87 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻².

items.stem: Spectrometry from a stellar intensity interferometer shows that a blackbody bright southern-sky reference star has total bolometric luminosity 6.894 × 10²⁹ W and a blackbody spectrum peaking at wavelength 250 nm. Take Wien's constant b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What is the radius of the star?
items.workedSolution: By Wien's law, T = b / λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (250 × 10⁻⁹) = 1.16 × 10⁴ K. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 7.31 × 10⁹ m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds T = 1.16 × 10⁴ K via Wien's law and R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 7.31 × 10⁹ m.

items.stem: Determine the radiant flux density b = L / (4πd²) received at a calibrated bolometric detector from a spherical blackbody young open-cluster A-type star of radius 3.95 × 10⁹ m and surface temperature 14500 K located 1.11 × 10¹⁶ m away (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴).
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 4π R² σ T⁴ = 4π(3.95 × 10⁹)²(5.67 × 10⁻⁸)(14500)⁴ = 4.91 × 10²⁹ W. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = σ T⁴ (R / d)² = 3.17 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = 4πR²σT⁴ and b = L / (4πd²) to obtain 3.17 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻².

items.stem: Determine the peak emission wavelength (in nm) of a spherical blackbody eclipsing-binary primary component with surface temperature 5120 K, radius 1.51 × 10¹⁰ m, and observer distance 1.52 × 10¹⁶ m in an optical interferometry array (b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K).
items.workedSolution: Using Wien's displacement law, λ_max = b / T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 5120 = 5.66 × 10⁻⁷ m = 566 nm.

items.stem: Observations with an orbital bolometric photometer target a spherical blackbody blue-white main-sequence star Vega-analog of radius 3.95 × 10⁹ m and effective surface temperature 5120 K situated 4.5 × 10¹⁶ m from the detector. Take σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. What apparent brightness (radiant intensity) arrives at the detector?
items.workedSolution: Luminosity L = 4π R² σ T⁴ = 4π(3.95 × 10⁹)²(5.67 × 10⁻⁸)(5120)⁴ = 7.64 × 10²⁷ W. Apparent brightness b = L / (4π d²) = σ T⁴ (R / d)² = 3.00 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Uses L = 4πR²σT⁴ and b = L / (4πd²) to obtain 3.00 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻².

items.stem: The blackbody continuum of a evolved red-clump giant (radius 1.51 × 10¹⁰ m, distance 5.23 × 10¹⁶ m) corresponds to an effective photospheric temperature of 6390 K as recorded by an astrometric space mission. Take Wien's constant b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K. At what wavelength, in nm, does its emitted spectrum peak?
items.workedSolution: Using Wien's displacement law, λ_max = b / T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 6390 = 4.54 × 10⁻⁷ m = 454 nm.

items.stem: Determine the radius of a blackbody metal-poor halo giant star whose continuum emission peaks at 390.8 nm and whose bolometric luminosity measured via a wide-field photometric survey is 1.228 × 10²⁹ W. Use b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: By Wien's law, T = b / λ_max = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (390.8 × 10⁻⁹) = 7.42 × 10³ K. From L = 4π R² σ T⁴, R = √[L / (4π σ T⁴)] = 7.54 × 10⁹ m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds T = 7.42 × 10³ K via Wien's law and R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 7.54 × 10⁹ m.

items.stem: The blackbody continuum of a nearby M-dwarf flare star (radius 1.55 × 10¹⁰ m, distance 1.56 × 10¹⁶ m) corresponds to an effective photospheric temperature of 14800 K as recorded by a cooled CCD radiometer. Take Wien's constant b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K. At what wavelength, in nm, does its emitted spectrum peak?
items.workedSolution: Using Wien's displacement law, λ_max = b / T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / 14800 = 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m = 196 nm.

items.stem: Data from an infrared space observatory for a spherical blackbody cool K-type giant Aldebaran-analog situated 5.09 × 10¹⁶ m from the detector show a spectral peak at λ_max = 400 nm and received radiant flux density 1.289 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻² (b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴).
items.workedSolution: (a) Wien's law gives T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (400 × 10⁻⁹) = 7.25 × 10³ K. (b) Inverse-square law gives L = 4π d² b_app = 4.20 × 10²⁹ W. (c) Stefan-Boltzmann law gives R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 1.46 × 10¹⁰ m.

items.stem: Data from an ultraviolet sky survey for a spherical blackbody hot B-type Orion-association star situated 1.96 × 10¹⁶ m from the detector show a spectral peak at λ_max = 489 nm and received radiant flux density 1.038 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻² (b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴).
items.workedSolution: (a) Wien's law gives T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (489 × 10⁻⁹) = 5.93 × 10³ K. (b) Inverse-square law gives L = 4π d² b_app = 5.01 × 10²⁸ W. (c) Stefan-Boltzmann law gives R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 7.54 × 10⁹ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts nm to m and applies T = b / λ_max.
Rearranges L = 4π R² σ T⁴ for R.

items.stem: At distance 2.48 × 10¹⁶ m, a luminous F-type subgiant behaves as an ideal blackbody radiator whose emission peaks at 453.8 nm and delivers apparent brightness 2.398 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻² to a space-based spectrometer. Use b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) Wien's law gives T = 2.90 × 10⁻³ / (453.8 × 10⁻⁹) = 6.39 × 10³ K. (b) Inverse-square law gives L = 4π d² b_app = 1.85 × 10²⁸ W. (c) Stefan-Boltzmann law gives R = √[L/(4πσT⁴)] = 3.95 × 10⁹ m.

markScheme.criterion: Converts nm to m and applies T = b / λ_max.
Rearranges L = 4π R² σ T⁴ for R.

items.stem: In a Neptune–Triton-analog planetary pair separated by 2.69 × 10⁸ m between centres, Ice Giant has mass 5.67 × 10²⁴ kg (radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) and Retrograde Moon has mass 6.3 × 10²³ kg (radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m). Referencing potential to zero at infinity and taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate V_g at the gravitational null point.
items.workedSolution: At the zero-field point x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 2.02 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -2.50 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -2.50 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Along the line joining World P (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) and World Q (mass 9.55 × 10²³ kg, radius 2.09 × 10⁶ m) separated centre-to-centre by 4.03 × 10⁸ m, a 900 kg ballistic research capsule is at distance 2.22 × 10⁸ m from World P's centre. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the magnitude of the resultant gravitational field due to both bodies at the ballistic research capsule?
items.workedSolution: Between the two centres, the gravitational fields oppose: |g_net| = |G M₁ / x² − G M₂ / (d − x)²| = |0.00808 − 0.00194| = 0.00614 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field magnitudes to obtain 0.00614 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Along the 3.84 × 10⁸ m line of centres of a terrestrial bi-planetary system, Planet Major (6.87 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) and Planet Minor (2.75 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m) create a zero-field saddle point. Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², find the total gravitational potential there.
items.workedSolution: At the zero-field point x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 3.20 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -1.72 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -1.72 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Determine the least initial speed at World P's surface (8.36 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) enabling a ballistic ballistic research capsule to reach World Q (2.32 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.83 × 10⁶ m) across a 4.61 × 10⁸ m centre-to-centre baseline (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Surface potential at x = R₁ is V(R₁) = −GM₁/R₁ − GM₂/(d − R₁) = -1.03 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹. Null-point potential at x₀ = 3.95 × 10⁸ m is V(x₀) = -1.65 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Potential barrier ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 1.01 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹, so v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.42 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) and v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.42 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Along the axis connecting Host World (8.95 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m) and Icy Moon (2.49 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m) in a super-Earth and its captured icy satellite of separation 5.38 × 10⁸ m, locate the zero-field coordinate measured from the centre of Host World.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 4.61 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 4.61 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: Determine the net gravitational field magnitude acting on a 2100 kg deep-space relay probe positioned at x = 2.85 × 10⁸ m from Ice Giant (1.31 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) along the 6.34 × 10⁸ m baseline to Retrograde Moon (1.07 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 2.09 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Between the two centres, the gravitational fields oppose: |g_net| = |G M₁ / x² − G M₂ / (d − x)²| = |0.0108 − 5.86 × 10⁻⁴| = 0.0102 N kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts opposing inverse-square field magnitudes to obtain 0.0102 N kg⁻¹.

items.stem: From the airless surface of Primary Planet (mass 1.55 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m), a cislunar transfer probe is fired along the line of centres toward Companion Moon (mass 2.42 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.83 × 10⁶ m) at separation 2.77 × 10⁸ m. Using G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², determine the threshold launch speed to cross the null-point barrier.
items.workedSolution: Surface potential at x = R₁ is V(R₁) = −GM₁/R₁ − GM₂/(d − R₁) = -1.41 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹. Null-point potential at x₀ = 2.46 × 10⁸ m is V(x₀) = -4.72 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Potential barrier ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 1.36 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹, so v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.65 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) and v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.65 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Primary (mass 1.55 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) and Exomoon (mass 1.72 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m) have a centre-to-centre separation of 3.35 × 10⁸ m in a sub-Neptune and its massive exomoon. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and zero potential at infinity. What is the combined gravitational potential at the collinear point where the resultant gravitational field is zero?
items.workedSolution: At the zero-field point x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 2.51 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -5.48 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -5.48 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Two spherical bodies in a Pluto–Charon-type dwarf-planet binary — Dwarf Planet A (5.22 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m) and Companion B (6.44 × 10²² kg, radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m) — lie 2.96 × 10⁸ m apart between centres. How far from Dwarf Planet A's centre do their gravitational fields cancel?
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 2.66 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 2.66 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: Along the axis connecting Primary (6.14 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) and Exomoon (3.84 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m) in a sub-Neptune and its massive exomoon of separation 4.15 × 10⁸ m, locate the zero-field coordinate measured from the centre of Primary.
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 3.32 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 3.32 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: In a Neptune–Triton-analog planetary pair separated by 2.85 × 10⁸ m between centres, Ice Giant has mass 8.6 × 10²⁴ kg (radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m) and Retrograde Moon has mass 1.76 × 10²³ kg (radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m). Referencing potential to zero at infinity and taking G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², calculate V_g at the gravitational null point.
items.workedSolution: At the zero-field point x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 2.49 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -2.63 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -2.63 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Neglecting rotation in a super-Earth and its captured icy satellite of centre-to-centre separation 3.45 × 10⁸ m, calculate the minimum surface launch speed from Host World (1.29 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) needed for an unpowered inter-moon cargo ferry to surmount the potential saddle and reach Icy Moon (2.02 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.83 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: Surface potential at x = R₁ is V(R₁) = −GM₁/R₁ − GM₂/(d − R₁) = -1.17 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹. Null-point potential at x₀ = 3.07 × 10⁸ m is V(x₀) = -3.16 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Potential barrier ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 1.14 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹, so v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.51 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) and v_min = √(2ΔV) = 1.51 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In a tidally locked binary rocky worlds, World P (mass 1.1 × 10²⁵ kg, radius 5.41 × 10⁶ m) and World Q (mass 3.06 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m) have a centre-to-centre separation of 6.52 × 10⁸ m. At what distance from the centre of World P along the line joining their centres is the resultant gravitational field strength zero?
items.workedSolution: Equating opposing field magnitudes G M₁ / x₀² = G M₂ / (d − x₀)² gives (d − x₀)/x₀ = √(M₂/M₁), so x₀ = [√M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂)] d = 5.59 × 10⁸ m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses x₀ = d √M₁ / (√M₁ + √M₂) to obtain 5.59 × 10⁸ m.

items.stem: A ballistic ballistic research capsule launches from the surface of World P (mass 4.3 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m) directly toward World Q (mass 2.69 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.83 × 10⁶ m), whose centre lies 4.88 × 10⁸ m away (ignore rotation and atmosphere; G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²). What minimum launch speed allows the ballistic research capsule to pass the gravitational null point and fall onto World Q?
items.workedSolution: Surface potential at x = R₁ is V(R₁) = −GM₁/R₁ − GM₂/(d − R₁) = -4.51 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. Null-point potential at x₀ = 3.90 × 10⁸ m is V(x₀) = -9.18 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Potential barrier ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) = 4.41 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹, so v_min = √(2ΔV) = 9.40 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔV = V(x₀) − V(R₁) and v_min = √(2ΔV) = 9.40 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Determine the net scalar gravitational potential (zero at infinity) at the collinear saddle point of zero field between Major Moon (6.0 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 7.33 × 10⁶ m) and Minor Moon (2.4 × 10²³ kg, radius 1.57 × 10⁶ m), whose centres lie 5.89 × 10⁸ m apart (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²).
items.workedSolution: At the zero-field point x₀ = d√M₁/(√M₁ + √M₂) = 4.91 × 10⁸ m, scalar potentials add negatively: V_g(x₀) = −GM₁/x₀ − GM₂/(d − x₀) = −(G/d)(√M₁ + √M₂)² = -9.78 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sums both negative scalar potentials at x₀ to obtain -9.78 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
